title: Nationalism in India
summary: This chapter connects nationalism to anti colonial movements, showing how the First World War, the Rowlatt Act, the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and the Khilafat issue combined to launch the Non Cooperation Movement of 1920 to 1922 under Mahatma Gandhi. Gandhi's satyagraha had already proved itself in Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad. The movement united students and lawyers in towns, Baba Ramchandra's peasants in Awadh, Alluri Sitaram Raju's tribal rebels in the Gudem Hills and plantation workers in Assam, each imagining swaraj in their own way. After the violence of Chauri Chaura in 1922, politics shifted through the Swaraj Party, the Simon Commission and the Lahore session of 1929 which demanded Purna Swaraj. The Salt March of March and April 1930 began the Civil Disobedience Movement, in which Patidars, Jats, merchants, industrialists and women participated in different ways, each with their own idea of freedom. The chapter also examines the limits of the movement: Dalit leaders like Ambedkar demanding separate electorates, the Poona Pact of 1932, and Muslim alienation. Finally it shows how Bharat Mata, folklore, the swaraj flag and reinterpreted history created a sense of collective belonging that bound Indians into one imagined nation.

sections.heading: The First World War, Its Aftermath and the Coming of Gandhi
sections.para: The First World War created a new economic and political situation in India. It led to a huge increase in defence expenditure which was financed by war loans and by increasing taxes: customs duties were raised and income tax was introduced. Through the war years prices increased, doubling between 1913 and 1918, which hit the common people hard. Villages were called upon to supply soldiers, and the forced recruitment in rural areas caused widespread anger. In 1918 to 19 and again in 1920 to 21, crops failed in many parts of India, resulting in acute shortages of food, and this was accompanied by an influenza epidemic. According to the census of 1921, twelve to thirteen million people perished as a result of famines and the epidemic. People hoped that their hardships would end after the war was over, but that did not happen, and this strengthened the demand for self rule. It was in this atmosphere that Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, who had returned to India from South Africa in January 1915, introduced the novel method of satyagraha, which emphasised the power of truth and the need to search for truth, suggesting that if the cause was true and the struggle was against injustice, physical force was not necessary to fight the oppressor.
points: The First World War led to a huge increase in defence expenditure which was financed by war loans and by increasing taxes, with customs duties raised and income tax introduced.
Prices doubled between 1913 and 1918, hitting the common people very hard during the war years.
Forced recruitment of soldiers in rural areas caused widespread anger among the village population.
Crops failed in 1918 to 19 and again in 1920 to 21, causing acute shortages of food across many parts of India.
An influenza epidemic accompanied the famines, and according to the census of 1921, twelve to thirteen million people perished.
People hoped their hardships would end after the war, but this did not happen, deepening resentment against British rule.
Mahatma Gandhi returned to India from South Africa in January 1915 and introduced the novel method of satyagraha in Indian politics.
Satyagraha emphasised the power of truth and suggested that physical force was not necessary to fight the oppressor if the cause was true.

keyTerms.meaning: Gandhi's method emphasising the power of truth and non violence in the struggle against injustice.
The colonial process by which villagers in rural areas were made to join the army during the First World War.
Tax introduced on incomes to finance war expenditure, first imposed during the First World War.

sections.trick: War years recipe: Taxes up, Prices double, Recruits forced, Crops fail, Flu kills millions. Then Gandhi lands in 1915 with truth as his weapon. Remember TPRCF.
sections.examPointer: Why did the First World War create hardship in India is a standard 3 marker, and the three early satyagraha movements are asked as 1 and 3 markers.

sections.heading: Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad: The Early Satyagrahas
sections.para: Gandhi tested the weapon of satyagraha in three famous movements before launching any all India struggle. In 1917 he travelled to Champaran in Bihar to inspire the peasants to struggle against the oppressive plantation system of indigo planters, whose contracts kept the peasants in bondage. That same year he organised a satyagraha to support the peasants of the Kheda district of Gujarat, where crop failure and a plague epidemic had made it impossible for the peasants to pay the revenue and they demanded that revenue collection be relaxed. In 1918, Mahatma Gandhi went to Ahmedabad to organise a satyagraha movement amongst the cotton mill workers, whose wages and working conditions had worsened. In all three cases Gandhi insisted that the struggle be peaceful, that volunteers be disciplined and that the oppressor be persuaded rather than crushed, for a satyagrahi wins through the goodness of the truth of his cause. These local successes gave Gandhi prestige and showed the Indian public that the British could be fought without arms, preparing the ground for the all India agitations of 1919. They also built the network of volunteers and local leaders which later carried the Non Cooperation and Civil Disobedience movements into the countryside.
points: In 1917 Gandhi travelled to Champaran in Bihar to inspire the peasants to struggle against the oppressive indigo plantation system.
In the same year, 1917, he organised a satyagraha to support the peasants of Kheda district in Gujarat after crop failure and a plague epidemic.
The Kheda peasants demanded that revenue collection be relaxed because crops had failed and they could not pay.
In 1918 Gandhi organised a satyagraha movement amongst the cotton mill workers of Ahmedabad over their wages and conditions.
Gandhi insisted on discipline, truth and non violence, believing a satyagrahi wins through the goodness of his cause.
These movements established Gandhi's leadership among peasants, workers and the middle classes before 1919.
The local struggles built a nationwide network of volunteers which later carried the Non Cooperation and Civil Disobedience movements forward.

keyTerms.meaning: Gandhi's satyagraha in Bihar against the oppressive indigo plantation system.
Satyagraha in Gujarat supporting peasants who could not pay revenue after crop failure and plague.
Satyagraha organised by Gandhi amongst the cotton mill workers of Ahmedabad.

sections.trick: Chain CKA 1917-17-18: Champaran indigo, Kheda revenue, Ahmedabad mill workers. Picture Gandhi walking from fields to farms to factories.
sections.examPointer: Match the year with the movement or list the three early satyagraha movements with places; this is a favourite 3 marker and MCQ set.

sections.heading: The Rowlatt Act, Jallianwala Bagh and the Khilafat Movement
sections.para: Emboldened by its success, the colonial government decided to clamp down on nationalists. In 1919 the Rowlatt Act was hurriedly passed through the Imperial Legislative Council despite the united opposition of the Indian members. It gave the government enormous powers to repress political activities and allowed detention of political prisoners without trial for two years. Gandhi launched a nationwide satyagraha against the proposed Rowlatt Act, and on 6 April a hartal was organised, with workers going on strike in railway workshops and shops closing down. The British decided to clamp down: in Punjab martial law was imposed and General Dyer took command. On 13 April 1919 the infamous Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place when a crowd of villagers who had come to attend the Baisakhi fair was fired upon, as Dyer wanted to produce a moral effect and terrorise the satyagrahis. As the news spread, crowds took to the streets, government buildings were attacked, and the government responded with brutal repression: satyagrahis were forced to rub their noses on the ground, crawl on the streets and do salaam to sahibs, and villages were bombed in Gujranwala in Punjab. Seeing violence spread, Gandhi called off the movement. He then decided to launch a more broad based movement with Muslim support: the Khilafat issue, concerning the defeat of Ottoman Turkey and the position of the Khalifa, gave him the chance to unite Hindus and Muslims, and the Congress session at Calcutta in September 1920 decided to start non cooperation in support of Khilafat and swaraj.
points: The Rowlatt Act of 1919 was passed hurriedly through the Imperial Legislative Council despite the united opposition of Indian members.
The Act gave the government enormous powers to repress political activities and allowed detention of political prisoners without trial for two years.
Gandhi launched a nationwide satyagraha against the Act, and on 6 April 1919 a hartal was organised with strikes and closed shops.
Martial law was imposed in Punjab under General Dyer, and on 13 April 1919 the Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place on Baisakhi day.
Dyer fired on the crowd deliberately to produce a moral effect and terrorise the satyagrahis.
The government responded to protests with brutal repression: satyagrahis were humiliated and villages in Gujranwala were bombed.
Seeing violence spread, Gandhi called off the Rowlatt satyagraha and looked for a broader movement uniting Hindus and Muslims.
The Khilafat issue, supported by Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali, allowed the Congress at Calcutta in September 1920 to launch non cooperation in support of Khilafat and swaraj.

keyTerms.meaning: Law giving the government powers to repress political activity and detain prisoners without trial for two years.
Amritsar garden where General Dyer fired on a Baisakhi crowd on 13 April 1919, massacring hundreds.
British army officer who imposed martial law in Punjab and ordered firing at Jallianwala Bagh.
A stoppage of work and closing of shops as a form of protest, organised on 6 April 1919.
Organisation formed to defend the Khalifa of Turkey, led by Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali.
Movement to protect the Ottoman Khalifa which Gandhi joined to unite Hindus and Muslims against British rule.

sections.trick: RJBK chain: Rowlatt 1919, Jallianwala 13 April, Khilafat link to Non Cooperation. Dyer wanted a moral effect; Gandhi wanted a moral weapon. Remember 6 April hartal and 13 April massacre.
sections.examPointer: Why was the Rowlatt Act opposed, why did Gandhi call off the movement and why did he take up the Khilafat issue are repeated 3 and 5 markers; the dates 6 April and 13 April 1919 are classic MCQs.

sections.heading: Why Non Cooperation? Hind Swaraj and the Plan of the Movement
sections.para: Mahatma Gandhi's idea of non cooperation was worked out in his famous book Hind Swaraj, written in 1909, where he declared that British rule was established in India with the cooperation of Indians and had survived only because of this cooperation. If Indians refused to cooperate, British rule in India would collapse within a year and swaraj would come. Gandhi proposed that the movement should unfold in stages: it should begin with the surrender of titles that the government awarded, and a boycott of civil services, army, police, courts and legislative councils, schools and foreign goods. Then, in case the government used repression, a full civil disobedience campaign would be launched, in which people would refuse to pay taxes. Through the summer of 1920 Gandhi and Shaukat Ali toured extensively, mobilising popular support for the movement, but many within the Congress were concerned about the boycott of the council elections scheduled for November 1920, and they feared that the movement might lead to popular violence. In the months between September and December there was intense tussle within the Congress, and finally at the Congress session at Calcutta in September 1920 the Non Cooperation programme was accepted, and it was confirmed at the Nagpur session in December 1920 with the support of leaders like Jawaharlal Nehru.
points: In his book Hind Swaraj of 1909, Gandhi declared that British rule was established and survived with the cooperation of Indians.
Gandhi argued that if Indians refused to cooperate, British rule would collapse within a year and swaraj would come.
The first stage of the movement was the surrender of titles that the government had awarded to Indians.
The second stage was a boycott of civil services, army, police, courts, legislative councils, schools and foreign goods.
If the government used repression, a full civil disobedience campaign would follow, in which people would refuse to pay taxes.
Through the summer of 1920 Gandhi and Shaukat Ali toured India widely, mobilising popular support for the movement.
Many within the Congress were worried about the boycott of the council elections of November 1920 and feared popular violence.
After intense debates the Calcutta session of September 1920 accepted the programme, and the Nagpur session of December 1920 adopted the Non Cooperation programme.

keyTerms.meaning: Book written by Gandhi in 1909 arguing that British rule survived on Indian cooperation and could be ended by non cooperation.
Movement of 1920 to 1922 in which Indians withdrew cooperation from British institutions step by step.
Refusal to take part in or use British institutions, goods and services as a weapon of protest.
Deliberate breaking of unjust colonial laws, planned as the later stage of Gandhi's movement.
Congress session of December 1920 which formally adopted the Non Cooperation programme.
Special Congress session of September 1920 which first accepted Gandhi's Non Cooperation proposal.

sections.trick: Gandhi's ladder: Titles down, Institutions shunned, Schools and courts shut, Goods burnt, finally Taxes refused. Remember the acronym TISGT for the stages, and the twin sessions Calcutta Sept plus Nagpur Dec 1920.
sections.examPointer: Why did Gandhi decide to withdraw cooperation and what were the stages of the movement form a classic 5 marker; the sessions of Calcutta and Nagpur 1920 are frequent MCQs.

sections.heading: The Movement in the Towns: Middle Class Participation
sections.para: The Non Cooperation Movement started with middle class participation in the cities. Thousands of students left government controlled schools and colleges, headmasters and teachers resigned, and lawyers gave up their legal practices. The council elections were boycotted in most provinces except Madras, where the Justice Party, the party of the non Brahmans, felt that entering the council was one way of gaining some power, something that usually only Brahmans had access to. The economic effects of the movement were significant: foreign goods were boycotted, liquor shops were picketed, and foreign cloth was burnt in huge bonfires. The import of foreign cloth halved between 1921 and 1922, its value dropping from one hundred and two crore rupees to fifty seven crore rupees. In many places merchants and traders refused to trade in foreign goods or finance foreign trade, and as the boycott movement spread and people began wearing only Indian clothes, the production of Indian textile mills and handlooms went up. However, the movement in the cities gradually slowed down for a variety of reasons: khadi cloth was often more expensive than mass produced mill cloth, and poor people could not afford it; similarly, the boycott of British institutions posed a problem, for there were no alternative Indian institutions to take their place, so students and teachers began trickling back to schools and lawyers joined back work in courts.
points: Thousands of students left government controlled schools and colleges, headmasters and teachers resigned, and lawyers gave up their legal practices.
The council elections of November 1920 were boycotted in most provinces except Madras, where the Justice Party of non Brahmans contested.
Foreign goods were boycotted, liquor shops were picketed and foreign cloth was burnt in huge bonfires across the towns.
The import of foreign cloth halved between 1921 and 1922, falling in value from one hundred and two crore rupees to fifty seven crore rupees.
Merchants and traders refused to trade in foreign goods or finance foreign trade as the boycott spread.
As people began wearing only Indian clothes, the production of Indian textile mills and handlooms went up.
The movement slowed in cities because khadi was expensive, poor people could not afford it, and mill cloth was cheaper.
The boycott of British institutions created a vacuum since no alternative Indian institutions existed, so students, teachers and lawyers gradually returned.

keyTerms.meaning: Refusal by Congress supported candidates to contest the November 1920 council elections as part of non cooperation.
Party of non Brahmans in Madras which entered the councils to gain power for groups usually excluded.
Form of protest by blocking or demonstrating outside shops, especially liquor shops and foreign cloth sellers.
Hand spun and hand woven cloth promoted by Gandhi as a symbol of self help and swadeshi.
Cloth imported from Britain whose value halved from one hundred and two crore to fifty seven crore rupees between 1921 and 1922.
The use of Indian made goods as a national duty and a weapon against British trade.

sections.trick: Towns boiled first: Students out, Titles surrendered, Courts shunned, Cloth burnt, Liquor picketed. Import fall 102 to 57 crore, like a cloth halved. The slowdown rhyme: khadi costly, no Indian institution ready.
sections.examPointer: Why did the Non Cooperation Movement gradually slow down in the cities is a very frequent 3 marker; the halving of foreign cloth imports is a repeated MCQ and data point in 5 markers.

sections.heading: Rebellion in the Countryside: Awadh and Baba Ramchandra
sections.para: In Awadh, peasants were led by Baba Ramchandra, a sanyasi who had earlier been to Fiji as an indentured labourer. The movement was against talukdars and landlords who demanded from peasants exorbitantly high rents and a variety of other cesses, and who made peasants perform begar, that is labour without payment. Peasants had to do begar and work at landlords' farms without any payment. As tenants they had no security of tenure and were regularly evicted so that they could acquire no right over the leased land. The peasant movement demanded reduction of revenue, abolition of begar and a social boycott of oppressive landlords. In many places nai dhobi bandhs were organised by panchayats to deprive landlords of the services of even barbers and washermen. In June 1920 Jawaharlal Nehru began going around villages in Awadh, talking to villagers and trying to understand their grievances, and by October the Oudh Kisan Sabha was set up, headed by Jawaharlal Nehru, Baba Ramchandra and a few others, with branches in over three hundred villages within a month. In 1921 the peasant movement developed in forms that the Congress leadership was unhappy with: houses of talukdars and merchants were attacked, bazaars were looted, and grain hoards were taken over, while local leaders told peasants that Gandhi had declared that no taxes were to be paid and land was to be redistributed among the poor.
points: In Awadh the peasant movement was led by Baba Ramchandra, a sanyasi who had earlier been to Fiji as an indentured labourer.
The movement was directed against talukdars and landlords who demanded exorbitantly high rents and a variety of other cesses.
Peasants were made to perform begar, that is labour without payment, on the farms of the landlords.
The demands included reduction of revenue, abolition of begar and a social boycott of oppressive landlords.
Nai dhobi bandhs organised by panchayats deprived landlords of the services of barbers and washermen.
In June 1920 Jawaharlal Nehru began village tours in Awadh and by October the Oudh Kisan Sabha was set up with him and Baba Ramchandra at its head.
Within a month the Oudh Kisan Sabha had branches in over three hundred villages.
In 1921 the movement turned militant: talukdars' houses were attacked, bazaars looted and grain hoards taken, with Gandhi's name invoked to sanction such action.

keyTerms.meaning: Sanyasi and former indentured labourer in Fiji who led the Awadh peasants against talukdars.
Landlords of Awadh who collected high rents and cesses from the peasants.
Compulsory labour without payment extracted from peasants by landlords.
Social boycott organised by panchayats denying landlords the services of barbers and washermen.
Peasant organisation set up in October 1920 headed by Jawaharlal Nehru and Baba Ramchandra.
Additional charges levied by landlords over and above the rent.
Protection of tenants from arbitrary eviction, which Awadh peasants lacked.

sections.trick: Awadh grievances: RRB, Rent high, Rend Begar, Revenues heavy, plus the barber and washerman bandh. Remember Baba from Fiji, Nehru touring June 1920, Sabha by October, three hundred villages.
sections.examPointer: Why did the Awadh peasant movement take militant forms and what were the demands of the peasants are common 3 markers; Baba Ramchandra and Oudh Kisan Sabha are MCQ favourites.

sections.heading: Tribal Peasants and Alluri Sitaram Raju in the Gudem Hills
sections.para: Tribal peasants interpreted the message of Mahatma Gandhi and the idea of swaraj in yet another way. In the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh a militant guerrilla movement spread in the early 1920s. The colonial government had closed large forest areas, preventing people from entering the forests to graze their cattle, or to collect fuelwood and fruits, which enraged the hill people whose livelihood was affected and who felt their traditional rights were being denied. When the government began forcing them to contribute begar for road building, they revolted. The leader of this movement was Alluri Sitaram Raju, who claimed that he had a variety of special powers: he could make correct astrological predictions and heal people, and he could survive even bullet shots. Captivated by Raju, the rebels proclaimed that he was an incarnation of God. Raju talked of the greatness of Mahatma Gandhi, said he was inspired by the Non Cooperation Movement, and persuaded people to wear khadi and give up drinking, but at the same time he asserted that India could be liberated only by the use of force and not through non violence. The Gudem rebels attacked police stations, attempted to kill British officials and carried on guerrilla warfare for achieving swaraj. Raju was captured and executed in 1924, and over time he became a folk hero.
points: Tribal peasants interpreted the message of Gandhi and the idea of swaraj in their own militant way.
The colonial government closed large forest areas, preventing tribals from grazing cattle, collecting fuelwood and gathering fruits.
When the government forced the hill people to contribute begar for road building, they revolted in the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh.
A militant guerrilla movement spread in the Gudem Hills in the early 1920s under Alluri Sitaram Raju.
Raju claimed special powers such as making correct astrological predictions, healing people and surviving bullet shots, and rebels proclaimed him an incarnation of God.
Raju talked of the greatness of Mahatma Gandhi, was inspired by the Non Cooperation Movement and persuaded people to wear khadi and give up drinking.
At the same time Raju asserted that India could be liberated only by force and not through non violence.
The rebels attacked police stations, tried to kill British officials and carried on guerrilla warfare; Raju was captured and executed in 1924, becoming a folk hero.

keyTerms.meaning: Tribal leader of the Gudem Hills guerrilla movement who combined admiration for Gandhi with armed struggle.
Region in Andhra Pradesh where the militant tribal movement spread in the early 1920s.
Mobile hit and hide fighting carried out by the Gudem rebels against the British.
Title given to Raju by the rebels who were captivated by his claimed powers.
Traditional rights of tribals to graze cattle and gather fuelwood and fruits, restricted by colonial forest laws.
Status Raju acquired after his capture and execution in 1924, remembered in local legend.

sections.trick: Raju's mix: Gandhi in mouth, gun in hand, khadi on body, powers in legend. Gudem equals guerrilla, execution 1924, folk hero forever. Remember GGP: Gudem, Gandhi, Guerrilla.
sections.examPointer: Why did tribal peasants revolt and describe the role of Alluri Sitaram Raju is a frequent 3 and 5 marker; his execution year 1924 is a common MCQ.

sections.heading: Swaraj in the Plantations
sections.para: Workers too had their own understanding of Mahatma Gandhi and the notion of swaraj. For plantation workers in Assam, freedom meant the right to move freely in and out of the confined space in which they were enclosed, and it meant retaining a link with the village from which they had come. Under the Inland Emigration Act of 1859, plantation workers were not permitted to leave the tea gardens without permission, and in fact permission was rarely granted. When they heard of the Non Cooperation Movement, thousands of workers defied the authorities, left the plantations and headed home. They believed that Gandhi Raj was coming and everyone would be given land in their own villages. They, however, never reached their destination: stranded on the way by a railway and steamer strike, they were caught by the police and brutally beaten up. Their visions of swaraj thus remained unfulfilled, yet the episode shows how the idea of freedom spread to the most confined corners of colonial society. Different social groups imagined swaraj differently, and this multiplicity of meanings, from peasants demanding land to workers demanding mobility, was the strength and also the complexity of the national movement.
points: For plantation workers in Assam, freedom meant the right to move freely in and out of the confined space in which they were enclosed.
Freedom also meant retaining a link with the village from which they had come to work on the plantations.
Under the Inland Emigration Act of 1859, plantation workers were not permitted to leave the tea gardens without permission, which was rarely granted.
Hearing of the Non Cooperation Movement, thousands of workers defied the authorities and left the plantations heading home.
The workers believed that Gandhi Raj was coming and everyone would be given land in their own villages.
Stranded on the way by a railway and steamer strike, the workers were caught by the police and brutally beaten up.
Their visions of swaraj remained unfulfilled, showing how different groups imagined freedom in their own way.
The episode demonstrates that swaraj had many meanings: land for peasants, mobility for workers, self rule for the middle classes.

keyTerms.meaning: Law preventing plantation workers from leaving the tea gardens without permission, which was rarely granted.
The imagined rule of Gandhi which tribals and workers believed would give them land and freedom.
Labourers in Assam tea gardens whose idea of swaraj was freedom of movement and a return home.
Province with tea plantations whose confined workers defied authorities during Non Cooperation.
Self rule, imagined differently by different groups as land, mobility or political freedom.

sections.trick: Assam workers dreamt of a walk home: One Act of 1859 locked the gates, Gandhi Raj opened them, the steamer strike broke the journey. Remember 1859 Act plus railway and steamer strike.
sections.examPointer: How did plantation workers interpret swaraj and what was the significance of the Inland Emigration Act 1859 are common 3 markers and MCQs.

sections.heading: Chauri Chaura, the Swaraj Party and the Road to Civil Disobedience
sections.para: In February 1922, Mahatma Gandhi decided to withdraw the Non Cooperation Movement because he felt the movement was turning violent in many places, and satyagrahis needed to be properly trained before they would be ready for mass struggles. The withdrawal disappointed many leaders, and within the Congress two trends emerged: Motilal Nehru and Chittaranjan Das formed the Swaraj Party within the Congress to argue for a return to council politics, while young leaders like Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose pressed for more radical mass agitation and for full independence. Two factors shaped Indian politics towards the late 1920s: the first was the worldwide economic depression, as agricultural prices began to fall from 1926 and collapsed after 1930, hitting the peasantry hard. The second was the failure of the Simon Commission, set up in 1928 to look into the functioning of the constitutional system in India and suggest changes, but which did not have a single Indian member, and was therefore greeted with the slogan Go back Simon in all parties. In October 1929 Lord Irwin made a vague offer of dominion status for India and a Round Table Conference, which did not satisfy Congress leaders. In December 1929, under the presidency of Jawaharlal Nehru, the Lahore Congress formalised the demand of Purna Swaraj or full independence for India, declaring that 26 January 1930 would be celebrated as Independence Day, but very few people took part in the celebrations and commitments wavered.
points: In February 1922 Gandhi withdrew the Non Cooperation Movement after the violence of Chauri Chaura, feeling satyagrahis needed proper training.
Motilal Nehru and Chittaranjan Das formed the Swaraj Party within the Congress arguing for a return to council politics.
Young leaders Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose demanded more radical mass agitation and full independence.
Agricultural prices began to fall from 1926 and collapsed after 1930, deepening the distress of the peasantry.
The Simon Commission of 1928 did not have a single Indian member and was greeted with the slogan Go back Simon.
In October 1929 Lord Irwin made a vague offer of dominion status and a Round Table Conference, which did not satisfy the leaders.
In December 1929 the Lahore Congress under Jawaharlal Nehru formalised the demand for Purna Swaraj or full independence.
Twenty six January 1930 was celebrated as Independence Day, but the celebrations drew few participants and commitments wavered.

keyTerms.meaning: Uttar Pradesh town where violence led Gandhi to withdraw the Non Cooperation Movement in February 1922.
Group formed by Motilal Nehru and Chittaranjan Das in 1923 to return to council politics.
All white constitutional commission without a single Indian member, boycotted with the slogan Go back Simon.
Complete independence demanded by the Lahore Congress session of December 1929.
Congress session under Jawaharlal Nehru's presidency that declared 26 January 1930 as Independence Day.
Viceroy whose vague offer of dominion status in October 1929 failed to satisfy Congress leaders.
Self governing status within the British Empire, offered vaguely by Irwin and rejected as inadequate.

sections.trick: After Chauri Chaura: Swaraj Party went in, Bose and Nehru pushed on, Simon came and was sent back, Irwin offered smoke, Lahore said Purna Swaraj. Remember 1922 withdrawal, 1928 Simon, 1929 Lahore, 26 January 1930.
sections.examPointer: Why was the Non Cooperation Movement withdrawn and how did the Lahore session of 1929 shape the Civil Disobedience Movement form a standard 5 marker; Chauri Chaura, Simon Commission and Purna Swaraj are guaranteed MCQs.

sections.heading: The Salt March and the Civil Disobedience Movement
sections.para: Mahatma Gandhi found in salt a powerful symbol that could unite the nation: it was something consumed by the rich and the poor alike, and the tax on it and the government monopoly over its production revealed the most oppressive face of British rule. On 31 January 1930 he sent a letter to Viceroy Irwin stating eleven demands, some of general interest and others specific to different classes, and the most stirring of all was the demand to abolish the salt tax. The letter was an ultimatum: if the demands were not fulfilled by 11 March, Congress would launch a civil disobedience campaign. The famous Salt March began on 12 March 1930 from the Sabarmati ashram to the Gujarati coastal town of Dandi, a distance of over two hundred and forty miles, with seventy eight trusted volunteers walking about ten miles a day for twenty four days. On 6 April 1930 Gandhi reached Dandi and ceremonially violated the law, manufacturing salt by boiling sea water. This marked the beginning of the Civil Disobedience Movement, in which people were asked not only to refuse cooperation with the British but also to break colonial laws. Thousands broke the salt law, manufactured salt and demonstrated in front of government salt factories; foreign cloth was boycotted and liquor shops were picketed; peasants refused to pay revenue and chaukidari taxes, village officials resigned and forest people violated forest laws. The government responded with brutal repression, arresting about one hundred thousand people including Abdul Ghaffar Khan and Gandhi himself. Finally the Gandhi Irwin Pact of 5 March 1931 allowed Gandhi to attend the Second Round Table Conference in London, which failed, and the movement was relaunched but gradually lost momentum by 1934.
points: Gandhi chose salt as the powerful symbol of the movement because it was consumed by rich and poor alike and the salt tax revealed the most oppressive face of British rule.
On 31 January 1930 Gandhi sent a letter to Viceroy Irwin stating eleven demands, the most stirring being the abolition of the salt tax.
The Salt March began on 12 March 1930 from the Sabarmati ashram with seventy eight volunteers and covered over two hundred and forty miles in twenty four days.
On 6 April 1930 Gandhi reached Dandi and ceremonially violated the salt law by manufacturing salt from boiling sea water.
The Civil Disobedience Movement differed from Non Cooperation because people were asked to break colonial laws, not merely refuse cooperation.
Peasants refused to pay revenue and chaukidari taxes, village officials resigned, and forest people violated forest laws by entering Reserved Forests.
The government arrested about one hundred thousand people, including Abdul Ghaffar Khan in April 1930 and Mahatma Gandhi himself.
The Gandhi Irwin Pact of 5 March 1931 led to the Second Round Table Conference, which failed, and the relaunched movement lost momentum by 1934.

keyTerms.meaning: Gandhi's march of 12 March to 6 April 1930 from Sabarmati to Dandi, breaking the salt law and starting Civil Disobedience.
Coastal town in Gujarat where Gandhi violated the salt law on 6 April 1930.
Movement from 1930 in which Indians broke colonial laws, especially the salt law, along with boycotts.

sections.heading: How Different Groups Participated and What They Wanted
sections.para: Different social groups joined the Civil Disobedience Movement with their own hopes. For rich peasant communities such as the Patidars of Gujarat and the Jats of Uttar Pradesh, swaraj meant a struggle against high revenues: as producers of commercial crops they were hit hard by the trade depression and falling prices, and they could not pay the revenue demand. But when the movement was called off in 1931 without the revenue rates being revised, many refused to participate when it was relaunched in 1932. For merchants and industrialists, led by Purshottamdas Thakurdas and G. D. Birla, swaraj meant freedom to expand trade and industry: they organised the Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress in 1920 and the Federation of the Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industries, FICCI, in 1927, attacked colonial control of the Indian economy and supported the movement with money and boycotts, though after the failure of the Round Table Conference their enthusiasm cooled due to fear of militant activities and growing socialism. The industrial working classes participated selectively, adopting Gandhian ideas such as boycott of foreign goods; railway workers struck in 1930 and dockworkers in 1932, but the Congress was reluctant to include workers' demands as part of its programme of struggle, fearing it would alienate industrialists. Women participated on a large scale, manufacturing salt, picketing foreign cloth and liquor shops and going to jail in thousands, though Gandhi and the Congress saw their primary role as domestic and gave them no position of real authority.
points: Rich peasants like the Patidars of Gujarat and the Jats of Uttar Pradesh joined as producers of commercial crops ruined by depression and falling prices.
For rich peasants swaraj meant a fight against high revenues, and when rates were not revised in 1931 many stayed away from the relaunched movement.
Merchants and industrialists supported the movement to gain protection against imports and a favourable rupee sterling foreign exchange ratio.
The Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress of 1920 and FICCI of 1927, led by Purshottamdas Thakurdas and G. D. Birla, attacked colonial control of the economy.
Industrial working classes participated selectively, with railway workers striking in 1930 and dockworkers in 1932, mostly in the Nagpur region.
The Congress was reluctant to include workers' demands for higher wages and better conditions for fear of alienating industrialists and dividing anti imperial forces.
Women participated in large numbers, manufacturing salt, picketing foreign cloth and liquor shops and courting arrest, many coming from high caste urban families or rich peasant households.
Gandhi saw national service as a sacred duty for women but believed their domestic duties were primary, so the Congress gave them no real position of authority.

keyTerms.meaning: Rich peasant communities of Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh who joined Civil Disobedience against high revenue.
Federation of the Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industries, formed by business leaders in 1927.

keyTerms.term: Purshottamdas Thakurdas and G. D. Birla
keyTerms.meaning: Industrialist leaders who attacked colonial control of the Indian economy and supported the Congress.
Exchange ratio industrialists wanted changed to discourage cheap imports.
Large scale participation of women in salt making, picketing and jail going during Civil Disobedience.
Pattern by which industrial workers adopted parts of the movement, like boycotts, without joining fully.

sections.trick: Four faces of swaraj: Patidar wants low revenue, Birla wants business, worker wants wages, woman wants dignity. Remember PRBW and that each group left when its demand was denied.
sections.examPointer: Why did different social groups participate in the Civil Disobedience Movement is a repeated 5 marker; FICCI 1927, the two industrialist leaders and the role of women are frequent 1 and 3 markers.

sections.heading: The Limits of Civil Disobedience: Dalits and Muslims
sections.para: The Civil Disobedience Movement had limits, shown most clearly in the position of Dalits and Muslims. For long the Congress had ignored the Dalits, or untouchables, for fear of offending the conservative high caste Hindus, the sanatanis. Gandhi called them harijan or children of God, organised satyagrahas for their entry into temples and access to public wells, tanks, roads and schools, and persuaded upper castes to change their hearts. But many Dalit leaders were keen on a different political solution: they wanted reservation of seats in educational institutions and a separate electorate, and Dalit participation in the movement was thus limited, though strong in Maharashtra and Nagpur where their organisation was strong. Dr B. R. Ambedkar organised the Dalits into the Depressed Classes Association in 1930, clashed with Gandhi at the Second Round Table Conference by demanding separate electorates for Dalits, and when the British conceded the demand, Gandhi began a fast unto death, believing separate electorates would slow down the process of their integration into society. Ambedkar ultimately accepted Gandhi's position, and the Poona Pact of September 1932 gave the Depressed Classes reserved seats in provincial and central legislative councils, but they were to be voted in by the general electorate. Similarly, after the decline of the Non Cooperation Khilafat movement, large sections of Muslims felt alienated from the Congress, relations between Hindus and Muslims worsened, and attempts at negotiation, such as those by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, failed when leaders like M. R. Jayakar of the Hindu Mahasabha opposed compromise, so large sections of Muslims could not respond to the call for a united struggle.
points: The Congress had for long ignored the Dalits for fear of offending the conservative high caste Hindus known as sanatanis.
Gandhi called the untouchables harijan, children of God, and organised satyagrahas for their entry into temples and access to wells, tanks, roads and schools.
Many Dalit leaders demanded reservation of seats in educational institutions and a separate electorate rather than symbolic equality.
Dr B. R. Ambedkar organised the Dalits into the Depressed Classes Association in 1930 and demanded separate electorates at the Second Round Table Conference.
When the British conceded separate electorates, Gandhi began a fast unto death, believing this would slow the integration of Dalits into society.
The Poona Pact of September 1932 gave the Depressed Classes reserved seats in provincial and central legislative councils but with voting by the general electorate.
After the decline of the Non Cooperation Khilafat movement, large sections of Muslims felt alienated and Hindu Muslim relations worsened.
Muhammad Ali Jinnah's compromise offer failed when M. R. Jayakar of the Hindu Mahasabha strongly opposed it, so Muslims could not respond to calls for a united struggle.

keyTerms.meaning: Children of God, the name Gandhi used for the untouchables whom he wanted integrated into society.
Conservative high caste Hindus whose sensibilities the Congress feared to offend.
Dalit leader who organised the Depressed Classes Association in 1930 and demanded separate electorates.
System in which Dalits or Muslims would elect their own representatives separately from the general electorate.
Agreement between Gandhi and Ambedkar giving reserved seats to the Depressed Classes with general electorate voting.
Muslim League leader willing to give up separate electorates if Muslims got reserved seats and proportional representation.
Hindu Mahasabha leader who strongly opposed efforts at Hindu Muslim compromise in 1928.
Organisation formed by Ambedkar in 1930 to politically represent the Dalits.

sections.trick: Two missing pillars: Ambedkar wanted separate electorates, Jinnah wanted reserved seats; Gandhi fasted, Poona Pact 1932 sealed reserved seats, Jayakar blocked Muslim compromise. Remember A J G P for the chain.
sections.examPointer: Examine the limits of the Civil Disobedience Movement with respect to Dalits and Muslims is a very high probability 5 marker; the Poona Pact 1932 and separate electorates are repeated MCQs.

sections.heading: The Sense of Collective Belonging: Bharat Mata, Folklore, Flag and History
sections.para: Nationalism spreads when people begin to believe that they are all part of the same nation, and nationalists in India worked to create this feeling. Images of Bharat Mata helped in creating this identity: the image was first created by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, who in the 1870s wrote Vande Mataram as a hymn to the motherland, later included in his novel Anandamath and widely sung during the Swadeshi movement in Bengal. Abanindranath Tagore painted his famous image of Bharat Mata, portrayed as an ascetic figure, calm, composed, divine and spiritual. Ideas of nationalism also developed through a movement to revive Indian folklore: nationalists toured villages to gather folk songs and legends, believing that folk tales revealed the true picture of traditional culture that had been corrupted and damaged by outside forces. Icons and symbols were another means: during the Swadeshi movement in Bengal a tricolour flag of red, green and yellow was designed, with eight lotuses representing eight provinces of British India and a crescent moon representing Hindus and Muslims; by 1921 Gandhi had designed the Swaraj flag, a tricolour of red, green and white with a spinning wheel in the centre, representing the Gandhian ideal of self help. Finally, history was reinterpreted: Indians looked into the past to discover their great achievements in art and architecture, science and mathematics, religion and culture, law and philosophy, crafts and trade, though this periodisation into Hindu, Muslim and British eras dangerously communalised history.
points: The image of Bharat Mata was first created by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, who wrote Vande Mataram in the 1870s as a hymn to the motherland.
Vande Mataram was later included in Bankim's novel Anandamath and was widely sung during the Swadeshi movement in Bengal.
Abanindranath Tagore painted his famous image of Bharat Mata as an ascetic figure that was calm, composed, divine and spiritual.
Nationalists toured villages to gather folk songs and legends, believing folklore revealed the true traditional culture corrupted by outside forces.
The Swadeshi movement in Bengal designed a tricolour flag of red, green and yellow with eight lotuses for eight provinces and a crescent moon for Hindus and Muslims.
In 1921 Gandhi designed the Swaraj flag, a tricolour of red, green and white with a spinning wheel in the centre representing self help.
Carrying the flag during protest marches became a symbol of defiance and unity.
Nationalist writers reinterpreted history to glorify India's past achievements, but the Hindu, Muslim and British periodisation communalised history and made some communities outsiders.

keyTerms.meaning: Mother India, the female figure of the nation first created by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay and painted by Abanindranath Tagore.
Hymn to the motherland written in the 1870s, included in Anandamath and sung during Swadeshi.
Novel by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay containing the hymn Vande Mataram.
Painter of the famous Bharat Mata image showing the nation as a calm, divine, ascetic figure.
Tricolour of red, green and white with a spinning wheel, designed by Gandhi to represent self help.
Nationalist effort to collect folk songs and legends to recover true traditional culture and instil pride.
Reading of the Indian past to discover achievements and explain colonial decline, which also communalised the periods.

sections.trick: Four glues of the nation: Mata the mother, Melodies the folklore, Flag the colours, Memories the history. Chant MF, FM: Bankim wrote, Abanindranath painted, Gandhi spun the wheel in 1921.
sections.examPointer: How did the sense of collective belonging develop, with Bharat Mata, folklore, the flag and reinterpretation of history, is a guaranteed 5 marker; the designers and dates of the flags are common MCQs.

boardQuestions.question: What was satyagraha?
boardQuestions.answer: Satyagraha was the novel method of mass agitation introduced by Mahatma Gandhi, which emphasised the power of truth and the need to search for truth. It suggested that if the cause was true and the struggle was against injustice, physical force was not necessary to fight the oppressor.

boardQuestions.question: Why did the First World War create hardships for the people of India?
boardQuestions.answer: The war created a new economic and political situation. 1) Defence expenditure increased hugely and was financed by war loans and by increasing taxes, with customs duties raised and income tax introduced. 2) Prices doubled between 1913 and 1918, hitting common people very hard. 3) Forced recruitment of soldiers in rural areas caused widespread anger. To add to this, crops failed in 1918 to 19 and 1920 to 21, causing food shortages, and the influenza epidemic with famine killed twelve to thirteen million people as per the census of 1921. Since hardships did not end after the war, discontent deepened.

boardQuestions.question: Why did Gandhiji decide to launch a nationwide satyagraha against the proposed Rowlatt Act 1919? Explain any three reasons.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) The Rowlatt Act was hurriedly passed through the Imperial Legislative Council despite the united opposition of Indian members, showing the arrogance of the government. 2) It gave the government enormous powers to repress political activities and allowed detention of political prisoners without trial for two years, which destroyed basic civil liberties. 3) It came after war hardships like high prices and forced recruitment, so a repressive law intensified resentment. Gandhi therefore launched a nationwide satyagraha, organising a hartal on 6 April 1919, which saw workers going on strike, shops closing and rallies in many cities, and when the movement spread, the British responded with brutal repression including the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.

boardQuestions.question: Why did Mahatma Gandhi withdraw the Non Cooperation Movement? Explain.
boardQuestions.answer: In February 1922 Mahatma Gandhi decided to withdraw the Non Cooperation Movement. 1) The movement was turning violent in many places, and at Chauri Chaura in Gorakhpur a violent clash with police led to the burning of a police station, which violated the core principle of satyagraha. 2) Gandhi believed that the Indian masses were not yet ready for the discipline of non violence and that satyagrahis needed proper training before mass struggles could continue. 3) Continuing after such violence would corrupt the moral character of the movement, so he chose withdrawal despite the disappointment of many leaders, some of whom later formed the Swaraj Party to return to council politics.

boardQuestions.question: How did the Non Cooperation Movement spread in the countryside? Explain with reference to Awadh and the Gudem Hills.
boardQuestions.answer: Introduction: The Non Cooperation Movement spread from the towns to the countryside, where peasants and tribals interpreted the idea of swaraj in their own ways. Body: 1) Awadh: In Awadh the peasant movement was led by Baba Ramchandra, a sanyasi who had earlier been to Fiji as an indentured labourer. The movement was directed against talukdars and landlords who demanded exorbitantly high rents and a variety of other cesses, and made peasants perform begar or unpaid labour. The peasants demanded reduction of revenue, abolition of begar and a social boycott of oppressive landlords, and nai dhobi bandhs organised by panchayats deprived landlords of the services of barbers and washermen. By October 1920 the Oudh Kisan Sabha, headed by Jawaharlal Nehru and Baba Ramchandra, had set up branches in over three hundred villages within a month. 2) Gudem Hills: In the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh a militant guerrilla movement spread in the early 1920s under Alluri Sitaram Raju. The colonial government had closed large forest areas, depriving tribals of grazing and fuelwood, and forced them to contribute begar for road building, so they revolted. Raju claimed special powers and was proclaimed an incarnation of God; he praised Gandhi, urged khadi and abstinence from drink, but asserted that India could be liberated only by force. The rebels attacked police stations and carried on guerrilla warfare, and Raju was captured and executed in 1924, becoming a folk hero. Conclusion: Thus the countryside gave the movement energy and mass base, though its forms were often more militant than the Congress leadership desired.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the participation of the middle class in the Non Cooperation Movement in the cities. Why did the movement slow down there?
boardQuestions.answer: Introduction: The Non Cooperation Movement started with middle class participation in the cities and spread rapidly in its first phase. Body: 1) Educational institutions: Thousands of students left government controlled schools and colleges, headmasters and teachers resigned, and lawyers gave up their legal practices, while the council elections of November 1920 were boycotted in most provinces except Madras, where the Justice Party of non Brahmans contested. 2) Economic boycott: Foreign goods were boycotted, liquor shops were picketed and foreign cloth was burnt in huge bonfires. The import of foreign cloth halved between 1921 and 1922, its value dropping from one hundred and two crore rupees to fifty seven crore rupees, merchants refused to trade in or finance foreign trade, and as people wore only Indian clothes, the production of Indian textile mills and handlooms went up. 3) Reasons for the slowdown: The movement in the cities gradually slowed for a variety of reasons. Khadi cloth was often more expensive than mass produced mill cloth, so poor people could not afford to buy it. The boycott of British institutions posed a problem because there were no alternative Indian institutions to replace them, so students and teachers began trickling back to government schools and lawyers joined back work in government courts. Conclusion: Thus the energy of the cities declined because the economic alternatives promised by the movement could not yet be delivered, though the foundation for the later Civil Disobedience Movement had been laid.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the Salt March highlighting its significance as the beginning of the Civil Disobedience Movement.
boardQuestions.answer: Introduction: Mahatma Gandhi found in salt a powerful symbol that could unite the nation, since it was consumed by the rich and the poor alike, and the government monopoly over its manufacture and the tax on it revealed the most oppressive face of British rule. Body: 1) The ultimatum: On 31 January 1930 Gandhi sent a letter to Viceroy Irwin stating eleven demands, the most stirring of all being the abolition of the salt tax, and gave the ultimatum that if the demands were not fulfilled by 11 March, Congress would launch a civil disobedience campaign. 2) The March: The famous Salt March began on 12 March 1930 from the Sabarmati ashram to the Gujarati coastal town of Dandi, over two hundred and forty miles away, with seventy eight trusted volunteers walking about ten miles a day for twenty four days, with Gandhi telling them exactly what he expected and newspapers reporting every step. 3) Breaking the law: On 6 April 1930 Gandhi reached Dandi and ceremonially violated the law, manufacturing salt by boiling sea water, which marked the beginning of the Civil Disobedience Movement in which people were asked not only to refuse cooperation but also to break colonial laws. 4) The spread: Thousands broke the salt law, manufactured salt and demonstrated in front of government salt factories; foreign cloth was boycotted, liquor shops picketed, peasants refused to pay revenue and chaukidari taxes, village officials resigned and forest people violated forest laws. The government responded with brutal repression, arresting about one hundred thousand people, and the Gandhi Irwin Pact of 5 March 1931 followed. Conclusion: The Salt March thus transformed a pinch of salt into a national weapon, showing how a simple everyday commodity could defy an empire.

boardQuestions.question: Why did different social groups participate in the Civil Disobedience Movement? Explain the role of any three groups.
boardQuestions.answer: Introduction: The Civil Disobedience Movement drew different social groups, each with its own idea of swaraj and its own grievances against colonial rule. Body: 1) Rich peasants: Communities like the Patidars of Gujarat and the Jats of Uttar Pradesh were producers of commercial crops hit hard by the trade depression and falling prices after 1926, and being unable to pay the revenue demand they saw swaraj as a struggle against high revenues. When the movement was called off in 1931 without the revenue rates being revised, many refused to participate when it was relaunched in 1932. 2) Business classes: During the First World War Indian industrialists had accumulated profits and now wanted protection against imports and a favourable rupee sterling foreign exchange ratio. They organised the Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress in 1920 and FICCI in 1927, led by Purshottamdas Thakurdas and G. D. Birla, attacked colonial control of the economy, supported the movement with money and boycotts, but grew apprehensive after 1931 fearing militant activities and growing socialism among young Congressmen. 3) Women: Thousands of women came out to hear Gandhi, participated in protest marches, manufactured salt, picketed foreign cloth and liquor shops and went to jail, with urban participants often from high caste families and rural participants from rich peasant households. Yet Gandhi saw their domestic duties as primary and the Congress gave them no position of real authority. Conclusion: The movement was thus a coalition of different expectations, and when the Congress could not fulfil the specific demands of each group, their enthusiasm faded, which limited the movement.

boardQuestions.question: Examine the limits of the Civil Disobedience Movement with reference to the Dalits and the Muslims.
boardQuestions.answer: Introduction: The Civil Disobedience Movement, despite its mass character, failed to unite two major communities, the Dalits and the Muslims, and this limited its reach. Body: 1) Dalits: For long the Congress had ignored the Dalits or untouchables for fear of offending the sanatanis, the conservative high caste Hindus. Gandhi called them harijan, children of God, organised satyagraha for their entry into temples and access to public wells, tanks, roads and schools, and persuaded upper castes to change their hearts. But many Dalit leaders were keen on a different political solution, demanding reservation of seats in educational institutions and a separate electorate. Dr B. R. Ambedkar organised the Dalits into the Depressed Classes Association in 1930 and clashed with Gandhi at the Second Round Table Conference demanding separate electorates for Dalits. When the British conceded the demand, Gandhi began a fast unto death, believing separate electorates would slow the integration of Dalits into society. Ambedkar ultimately accepted Gandhi's position, and the Poona Pact of September 1932 gave the Depressed Classes reserved seats in provincial and central legislative councils but with voting by the general electorate. 2) Muslims: After the decline of the Non Cooperation Khilafat movement, large sections of Muslims felt alienated from the Congress, which was increasingly associated with openly Hindu religious nationalist groups. Relations between Hindus and Muslims worsened, and Muhammad Ali Jinnah's offer to give up separate electorates in return for reserved seats in the Central Assembly and proportional representation in Muslim dominated provinces was opposed by leaders like M. R. Jayakar of the Hindu Mahasabha. Conclusion: With suspicion and distrust on both sides, large sections of Muslims and Dalits did not join the call for a united struggle, showing the social limits of Indian nationalism during the 1930s.

boardQuestions.question: Read the extract: 'Mahatma Gandhi found in salt a powerful symbol that could unite the nation. The famous Salt March was started on 12 March 1930.' Answer: (a) Why did Gandhi choose salt? (b) Trace the route and the date of violation of the salt law. (c) How did the government respond?
boardQuestions.answer: (a) Gandhi chose salt because it was consumed by the rich and the poor alike, and the tax on it and the government monopoly over its production revealed the most oppressive face of British rule; salt was thus a symbol that could unite the entire nation. (b) The march began on 12 March 1930 from the Sabarmati ashram to Dandi, a coastal town of Gujarat over two hundred and forty miles away, with seventy eight volunteers walking for twenty four days, and on 6 April 1930 Gandhi ceremonially violated the law by manufacturing salt by boiling sea water. (c) The government responded with brutal repression: peaceful satyagrahis were attacked, women and children were beaten, about one hundred thousand people were arrested, including Abdul Ghaffar Khan and Mahatma Gandhi himself, which led to further protests such as the attack on government property in Sholapur.

boardQuestions.question: Read the extract: 'When they heard of the Non Cooperation Movement, thousands of workers defied the authorities, left the plantations and headed home.' Answer: (a) Who were these workers and where did they work? (b) What did freedom mean to them? (c) What was the outcome of their journey home?
boardQuestions.answer: (a) These were plantation workers in Assam who worked in tea gardens under confined conditions. (b) For them freedom meant the right to move freely in and out of the confined space in which they were enclosed, and retaining a link with the village from which they had come; they believed Gandhi Raj was coming and everyone would be given land in their own villages. (c) Under the Inland Emigration Act of 1859 they could not leave the tea gardens without permission, so their defiance was illegal; stranded on the way by a railway and steamer strike, they were caught by the police and brutally beaten up, so their visions of swaraj remained unfulfilled. The extract shows how different groups imagined the idea of freedom in their own way.

boardQuestions.question: Read the extract: 'Dr B. R. Ambedkar organised the Dalits into the Depressed Classes Association in 1930 and clashed with Mahatma Gandhi at the Second Round Table Conference.' Answer: (a) What did Ambedkar demand? (b) How did Gandhi react? (c) What was the Poona Pact?
boardQuestions.answer: (a) Ambedkar demanded separate electorates for the Dalits, so that the Depressed Classes could elect their own representatives, a demand he pressed at the Second Round Table Conference. (b) Gandhi began a fast unto death because he believed that separate electorates for Dalits would slow down the process of their integration into society, and the British concession to Ambedkar's demand triggered this fast. (c) The Poona Pact of September 1932 gave the Depressed Classes, later the Scheduled Castes, reserved seats in provincial and central legislative councils, but they were to be voted in by the general electorate; Ambedkar accepted the Pact under the pressure of Gandhi's fast, and Dalit participation in the Civil Disobedience Movement thus remained limited.

boardQuestions.question: How did people belonging to different communities, regions or language groups develop a sense of collective belonging in India?
boardQuestions.answer: Introduction: This sense of collective belonging came partly through the experience of united struggles, but several cultural processes were also involved, through which history, fiction, folklore, songs, popular prints and symbols played an important part. Body: 1) Image of Bharat Mata: The identity of India came to be visually associated with the image of Bharat Mata, first created by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, who in the 1870s wrote Vande Mataram as a hymn to the motherland later included in his novel Anandamath and widely sung during the Swadeshi movement in Bengal; Abanindranath Tagore painted the famous image of Bharat Mata as an ascetic figure, calm, composed, divine and spiritual. 2) Folklore: Nationalists toured villages and gathered folk songs and legends, believing that folk tales revealed the true picture of traditional culture that had been corrupted and damaged by outside forces, and that it was essential to preserve folk tradition in order to discover one's national identity and restore pride in one's past. 3) Icons and symbols: During the Swadeshi movement in Bengal a tricolour flag of red, green and yellow with eight lotuses for eight provinces and a crescent moon for Hindus and Muslims was designed, and by 1921 Gandhi had designed the Swaraj flag of red, green and white with a spinning wheel in the centre, and carrying the flag during marches became a symbol of defiance. 4) Reinterpretation of history: Indians looked into the past to discover their great achievements in art and architecture, science and mathematics, religion and culture, law and philosophy, crafts and trade, and felt that the British view of Indians as backward was false, though this Hindu Muslim British periodisation dangerously communalised history. Conclusion: These images, songs, flags and histories gave Indians one mother, one memory and one flag, binding diverse communities into a single imagined nation.

boardQuestions.question: Why did the relationship between the poor peasants and the Congress remain uncertain during the Civil Disobedience Movement?
boardQuestions.answer: 1) The poor peasants were small tenants cultivating land rented from landlords, and the depression made it impossible for them to pay their rent, so they wanted the unpaid rent to the landlord to be remitted. 2) They joined a variety of radical movements, often led by Socialists and Communists, whose demands the Congress did not share. 3) Apprehensive of raising issues that might upset the rich peasants and landlords, the Congress was unwilling to support no rent campaigns, so the relationship between the poor peasants and the Congress remained uncertain, and their demands were never fully adopted.
